blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

In an unsorted array, a value smaller than `a[mid]` can occur on either side of mid, and so can a larger value. A mismatch therefore proves only that mid is not the target; discarding either side can discard the answer.
Contrast the strategies

A scan checks every still-possible position and is O(n). Calling the proposed loop O(log n) describes how quickly it throws positions away, not whether those positions are impossible. Checking only mid or pretending the data is sorted makes the same unsupported elimination. Actual sorting would restore correctness but adds preprocessing that must be counted.
Complexity ranks correct algorithms; it cannot repair an invalid elimination rule.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: The midpoint comparison gives no legal direction in unsorted data, so the algorithm can discard the target.
One midpoint mismatch eliminates only that position; every other unsorted position can still contain the target.
The comparison direction is invalid until the data is actually ordered, and real sorting work must be counted.

feedback.reason: A correct O(n) scan is preferable to an unsound O(log n)-shaped procedure.

options.text: Use a linear scan because every position remains a possible target location.
Use the proposed binary search because O(log n) is asymptotically faster.
Check only the midpoint and return not found after one mismatch.
Treat the array as sorted without actually preprocessing it.

prompt: An unsorted array is searched once for an exact target. A proposed binary search compares the midpoint and discards one side as though the array were sorted. Which strategy is correct?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The complete predicate is `i is even AND a[i] is divisible by 7`. Increasing i flips parity at every step, while divisibility can appear at separated values, so truth can recur after a false midpoint even though `a` itself is sorted.
Contrast the strategies

Scan indices in increasing order and return the first index satisfying both clauses. Sorted value order alone does not make the conjunction monotonic; accepting either clause returns a contract-wrong record, and a false midpoint cannot certify either half. An added index over qualifying positions could change the representation.
Derive search structure from the whole predicate, including index and identity clauses.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: Sorted values do not make the combined index-and-divisibility condition monotonic.
A false midpoint does not imply every candidate on that side is false.
The query requires both parts and the first qualifying element.

feedback.reason: Correctness follows the complete query predicate, not a partial sorted-data signal.

options.text: Scan candidates because the full condition is not monotonic in sorted value order.
Binary-search the condition because the array values are sorted.
Return the first midpoint satisfying either part of the condition.
Discard the half containing a false midpoint.

prompt: A sorted array is queried for the first element whose index is even and whose value is divisible by 7. The condition can be true, false, then true again. Which approach is justified without additional structure?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The output says “any index,” so equality at any midpoint completes binary search and the first equal position found by a scan also completes the scan. Duplicate values do not add a leftmost or rightmost obligation that the prompt never requested.
Contrast the strategies

After both pass correctness, a random-access sorted array gives binary search O(log n) worst-case lookup versus O(n) scanning, while tiny inputs or surrounding costs can still influence implementation choice. “Only scan” and “only binary” confuse preference with legality; requiring the first occurrence silently changes the result contract.
Do not strengthen an any-match contract while evaluating candidate algorithms.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: A scan is also correct, though usually slower asymptotically.
The stated contract accepts any matching index and does not impose a first-occurrence boundary.
Duplicates do not prevent binary search from returning one key-equal index under an any-match contract.

feedback.reason: Correctness is a gate, not a ranking result.

options.text: Both are correct; compare workload and cost only after confirming the any-match contract.
The scan is the only correct method because duplicates exist.
Binary search is the only correct method because the input is sorted.
Both are incorrect unless they return the first occurrence.

prompt: A sorted array contains duplicates. The query asks for any index containing target. Both a standard binary search and a linear scan are implemented correctly. Which principle applies?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Sorting by key can reorder equal-key records. The leftmost equal record in the sorted array is defined by sorted position, not by the minimum arrival position, so neither any match nor the leftmost sorted duplicate proves the requested identity.
Contrast the strategies

Scanning the original sequence returns the first qualifying arrival by construction. Binary search becomes suitable only if the index preserves arrival positions and can select their minimum for each key. Ignoring the clause is not optimization; it changes the function’s observable result.
Key equality and record identity are separate proof obligations.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: A key match in sorted order does not establish the first arrival-order match.
The leftmost duplicate by key need not carry the smallest original arrival position.
Dropping the original-order clause returns a different result and therefore changes the required contract.

feedback.reason: The fastest key lookup is not correct if it returns the wrong identity under the output contract.

options.text: Scan the original sequence unless the sorted representation also preserves and exposes original-order provenance.
Binary-search the sorted array and return any matching record.
Binary-search and choose the leftmost sorted duplicate as the first arrival.
Ignore the original-order clause because binary search is faster.

prompt: A function must return the first matching record in original arrival order. Records are also available in a separate array sorted by key, but that array does not preserve arrival positions. Which strategy is correct for this output contract?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

With adjacent candidates `right = left + 1`, a lower-biased midpoint is `mid = left`. Executing `left = mid` leaves both bounds unchanged, so the next iteration repeats the same state and can run forever.
Contrast the strategies

Repair the interval convention and update together—for example, discard mid with `left = mid + 1`, or use the matching bias and invariant for a retained mid. Variable names and sorted input do not prove progress, and a nonterminating loop is not equivalent to a terminating scan.
For every nonterminal branch, prove that the active interval strictly shrinks.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: Sortedness can justify a direction but cannot repair an update that leaves the same interval active.
Variable names do not guarantee interval shrinkage or termination.
A scan advances to a new position; this defective loop can inspect the same midpoint forever.

feedback.reason: A claimed asymptotic benefit is irrelevant when the algorithm violates termination.

options.text: It is incorrect because it does not guarantee progress; a terminating scan is preferable until the boundary contract is repaired.
It is O(log n) because the expected variables are present.
It is correct whenever the input is sorted.
It is equivalent to a linear scan because both inspect values.

prompt: A binary-search implementation uses left, right, and mid but updates left = mid when the midpoint is too small and uses a lower-biased midpoint. On two adjacent candidates it can repeat forever. Which assessment is correct?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Strategy A performs one pass: O(n). Strategy B performs O(n) copying, O(n log n) comparison sorting, and O(log n) lookup, so `O(n + n log n + log n) = O(n log n)`.
Contrast the strategies

Both complete strategies are correct because B actually creates ordered data, but for one query O(n) grows more slowly than O(n log n). Looking only at B’s final O(log n) query hides the work required to make that query legal; binary-searching without sorting is not a correct third option.
Compare end-to-end workload cost, not the cheapest stage of a pipeline.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: Without ordering, the midpoint comparison cannot prove which half excludes the target.
O(n log n) contains an additional unbounded logarithmic factor and therefore grows faster than O(n).
This ignores the preprocessing cost required to make binary search legal.

feedback.reason: The comparison must include every operation needed to produce a correct answer.

options.text: The scan, because O(n) is less than O(n log n + log n).
Sort plus binary search, because the final query is O(log n).
They are asymptotically equal.
Binary-search the unsorted array directly.

prompt: A one-time lookup is performed on an unsorted array of n values. Option A scans in O(n). Option B sorts a copy in O(n log n) and then binary-searches in O(log n). Ignoring constants, which strategy has the better complete asymptotic cost for this single query?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

A forward-only list reaches a midpoint by following links from a known node. Repeating this over sublists of sizes `n, n/2, n/4, ...` costs less than 2n total traversal work, so binary-style halving does not produce array-style O(log n) time.
Contrast the strategies

One forward traversal is O(n), can return on equality, and can stop after passing the target. Counting midpoint access as O(1), claiming all sorted structures are logarithmic, or relying on variable names ignores the representation’s operations. An auxiliary index or random-access copy would be a different representation.
Logical halving yields logarithmic time only when each iteration’s access cost supports it.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: Successive midpoint traversals can sum to linear work even though the logical interval halves.
The data structure does not provide random access.
Access cost and invariant, not names, determine the method.

feedback.reason: Correctness and cost both depend on the data-access contract.

options.text: Traverse linearly because locating the midpoint is not constant-time under this access model.
Apply array-style binary search and count each midpoint access as O(1).
Binary search remains O(log n) on every sorted structure.
Use whichever code has variables named left and right.

prompt: A linked list is sorted by value and supports only sequential traversal from the head. Which default strategy is more defensible for one exact lookup?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Binary search makes O(log W) candidate evaluations. At O(n) per evaluation, its total is `O(n) × O(log W) = O(n log W)`; returning a boolean does not make the work used to compute it free.
Contrast the strategies

The monotonicity proof makes binary search correct, but a direct O(n) pass that answers the same result contract is also correct and asymptotically cheaper for this single query. Ignoring predicate cost reports only the number of calls, while declaring the scan incorrect confuses the existence of an optimization pattern with exclusivity.
Multiply work per predicate by predicate calls before comparing legal strategies.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: The predicate cost must be multiplied by the number of iterations.
The boolean is the result of scanning n records, so each midpoint evaluation carries O(n) work.
Monotonicity enables binary search but does not invalidate a direct scan that satisfies the same output contract.

feedback.reason: A legal algorithm is not automatically the cheapest legal algorithm.

options.text: Binary search is correct, but its total cost is O(n log W); a direct O(n) scan may be cheaper if it answers the same contract.
Binary search costs only O(log W), regardless of predicate work.
A scan is automatically incorrect when a monotonic predicate exists.
Midpoint evaluation has no cost because it returns a boolean.

prompt: A monotonic predicate is proven correct, but evaluating it at one candidate scans all n records. Which statement best evaluates binary search versus one direct scan for a single query?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Both algorithms return the exact target correctly on the sorted array. For a tiny one-off input, setup, branch behavior, code already in place, and review simplicity can matter more than the asymptotic gap visible only as n grows.
Contrast the strategies

Correctness-first therefore admits both and leaves a measured engineering choice. Sortedness makes binary search legal rather than mandatory; small size can favor a scan without making it universally mandatory; size itself invalidates neither method.
After correctness, choose from the actual workload rather than a universal slogan.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: Sortedness makes exact binary search legal but does not make it the only correct implementation.
Input size changes practical cost but does not invalidate either correctly implemented method.
Binary search remains correct; the preference is an engineering tradeoff.

feedback.reason: Correctness narrows the candidate strategies; it does not always select a unique implementation.

options.text: Both pass correctness; choose using measured constants, simplicity, and surrounding workload rather than an absolute rule.
Binary search is mandatory because sorted input always requires it.
Linear scan is mandatory for all small inputs.
Neither can be correct on a small array.

prompt: A sorted array is tiny and queried once. Both scan and exact binary search are correct. What should the correctness-first framework conclude?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The replacement must state which answer candidates remain in the active interval, what each midpoint outcome proves, why every update preserves all possible answers and strictly shrinks the interval, and what the exit state returns.
Contrast the strategies

Without those obligations, an attractive benchmark may only measure a loop that silently discards valid answers on unseen inputs. The word “sorted” helps only if the full query follows that order, and renaming variables adds no invariant. Keep the verified scan until the proof and tests are complete.
Require invariant, elimination, progress, and exit proofs as one review packet.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: A benchmark cannot prove correctness on unseen inputs.
The query must align with the order and the implementation must preserve the invariant.
Names suggest a familiar shape but supply no candidate invariant, discard proof, or termination guarantee.

feedback.reason: Optimization requires a correctness argument before performance evidence is relevant.

options.text: Reject the replacement until a legal half-discard invariant and coherent boundary updates are supplied.
Accept it if one benchmark is faster.
Accept it because the requirement text contains the word sorted.
Rename variables to left, right, and mid.

prompt: A proposed optimization replaces a verified scan with binary search but cannot state which half is impossible after each mismatch. What should code review require?

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Query alignment creates a directional truth or comparison relation. Legal discard converts each midpoint result into proof that a complete region is answer-free. Coherent boundaries retain every possible answer while making strict progress to a defined exit.
Contrast the strategies

All three are necessary: semantic alignment without correct updates can loop or skip the boundary, while polished boundaries cannot repair a nonmonotonic query. A variable named mid establishes none of them. Compare total costs only among strategies that pass all correctness gates.
Prove both why a side is impossible and why the implementation removes exactly that side.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: A variable name describes syntax but proves neither query monotonicity, legal elimination, nor progress.
A legal idea can still be implemented incorrectly.
This is the correctness mechanism.
This establishes directional meaning.

feedback.reason: Binary search must pass semantic and mechanical correctness gates.

options.text: The query or predicate aligns monotonically with the ordered search domain.
Each midpoint result proves a complete region cannot contain the answer.
The interval updates preserve candidates and guarantee termination.
The implementation has a variable named mid.

prompt: Which conditions must be established before preferring binary search over a correct scan? Select all that apply.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

With unsorted data, every position remains possible. With an arbitrary condition, truth can recur on both sides of mid. With missing provenance, a key match may be the wrong record. A scan directly preserves each of those unresolved possibilities.
Contrast the strategies

Many exact queries on a stable random-access sorted array are the control case: the comparison is aligned, midpoint access is O(1), and preprocessing is already available, so binary search is both correct and well amortized. Selecting it as a scan-default case would ignore the workload’s supplied structure.
Use the method whose inspected order preserves every requirement the representation cannot summarize.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: This workload already supplies query-aligned order, random access, and reuse across many exact lookups.
No single boundary exists.
A sorted lookup may return the wrong identity.
No midpoint direction exists.

feedback.reason: Scanning remains correct when the query lacks the structure needed for safe elimination.

options.text: Unsorted data with one exact query and no legal preprocessing.
A condition that can change true and false repeatedly across the ordered input.
The output requires the first match in original order and the index does not preserve that provenance.
Many exact queries on a stable random-access sorted array.

prompt: Which scenarios make a linear scan the safer correct default? Select all that apply.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Unsupported discard can lose the only answer, nonprogress can prevent termination, and returning any key match can violate an original-order identity requirement. Each defect breaks the result or termination contract on an allowed input.
Contrast the strategies

A benchmark samples timing on exercised paths; it cannot legalize untested wrong paths. A larger constant factor is different: it can make a correct optimization unattractive on a machine or workload, but it does not by itself prove an incorrect result or nontermination.
Classify contract failures before comparing the speed of remaining legal implementations.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: This may affect preference but does not by itself invalidate correctness.
The target may be lost.
The algorithm may not terminate.
It violates the result contract.

feedback.reason: Correctness defects are categorical; performance disadvantages are comparative.

options.text: It discards a side without proving that side impossible.
Some branch can leave the active interval unchanged.
It returns any key match when the contract requires the first original-order match.
Its constant factor is larger than the scan on one machine.

prompt: Which defects invalidate a claimed binary-search optimization even if its average benchmark is fast? Select all that apply.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

An ordered representation can create a comparison-aligned domain, but it must retain every output field such as original position. A proven monotonic reformulation creates a boundary. A maintained query-specific index can provide both efficient access and required identity metadata.
Contrast the strategies

Each selected change adds real structure and carries build, update, storage, or proof costs that belong in the final comparison. Renaming a scan index to mid changes no ordering, predicate implication, access operation, or output contract.
A scan-to-search transfer requires a new invariant or representation, not a cosmetic rewrite.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

messages.text: Renaming the loop index adds no ordered domain, half-discard implication, or boundary invariant.
The access and lookup contract changes.
A searchable boundary may then exist.
This can create a legal query-aligned domain.

feedback.reason: The strategy can transfer when the data representation or predicate gains the missing elimination structure.

options.text: Build an ordered representation that preserves all required output provenance.
Reformulate the condition as a proven monotonic predicate.
Add a maintained index that supports the required key and identity query.
Rename the scan index to mid.

prompt: Which changes can make binary search appropriate where a scan was previously required? Select all that apply.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
The review sequence is:

items: State exactly which value or record identity must be returned, including first/last and no-result behavior.
For every candidate strategy, prove result correctness and termination on every allowed input.
For the strategies that remain, add preprocessing, access, predicate, query-volume, and output-production costs.
Choose using the complete workload and engineering constraints, then verify the selected implementation.

blocks.text: The cost comparison is defined only over strategies that satisfy the same complete contract.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

feedback.reason: Correctness precedes asymptotic and practical optimization.

elements.text: State the exact result and identity contract.

prompt: Arrange the strategy-review sequence for binary search versus linear scan.

Audit the replacement in dependency order:

feedback.reason: The replacement is an algorithmic proof obligation before it is a benchmark exercise.

prompt: Arrange the review of a proposed scan-to-binary-search replacement.

constraints: Comparison sorting is O(n log n).
The binary search is O(log n).

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Strategy A visits at most n values, so it is O(n). Strategy B costs `O(n)` to copy, `O(n log n)` to comparison-sort, and `O(log n)` to search. Summing gives `O(n + n log n + log n) = O(n log n)`.
Contrast the strategies

O(log n) describes only the final lookup after order exists. For one query, the sorting term dominates, so the correct direct scan has the better complete asymptotic time. O(n²) overstates comparison sorting, while O(n) for Strategy B incorrectly drops its sorting work.
Preprocessing must be amortized across enough reuse before its per-query benefit can matter.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

feedback.reason: For a single unsorted query, making binary search legal costs more asymptotically than scanning.

prompt: An unsorted array of n values receives one query. Strategy A scans once. Strategy B copies and comparison-sorts the array, then binary-searches it. Select the complete worst-case time for each strategy.

constraints: The binary-search predicate is evaluated independently at each candidate.
The direct scan needs one pass.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
Binary search makes O(log W) predicate calls and each independently scans n records, so its total is `O(log W) × O(n) = O(n log W)`. The direct method performs one O(n) pass.
Contrast the strategies

Both methods are legal by the prompt, but the logarithmic candidate count does not erase predicate work. O(log W) omits the n-record evaluation; O(n) for binary search omits repeated calls; O(nW) would count all W candidates rather than logarithmically many.
Count how often the expensive subroutine runs before calling a legal method faster.
blocks.title: Key takeaway

feedback.reason: Legality does not imply lower total cost.

prompt: A proven monotonic binary search examines O(log W) candidates, but one predicate evaluation scans n records. A direct legal scan answers the same question in O(n). Select the total time of both strategies.
